# GEOSENTRA — Project Report

**This file is the single source of truth for what GEOSENTRA currently does.** It is generated by reading the actual code in this repository, not by describing an intended design. If something below stops being true after a code change, this file must be corrected in the same change — see [Documentation maintenance checklist](#documentation-maintenance-checklist).

Last verified against commit: `3d279a4` (branch `main`) — re-checked, no frontend changes since, when the USP and Feasibility sections below were added.

---

## A. Project overview

GEOSENTRA is a **multi-hazard disaster-intelligence and relocation-planning prototype**. It helps a disaster authority identify which populated areas ("habitations") are at risk from landslide, flood, coastal erosion or cloudburst, understand the vulnerability of the people living there, evaluate safe relocation destinations against their real capacity limits, plan a safe travel route tailored to who is moving, and keep a record of decisions.

**This is a frontend-only prototype.** There is no backend server, no database, no live sensor feed, and no trained machine-learning model behind any screen. Every number is calculated in the browser from hand-authored mock data (`src/data/*.js`). Several files in `src/utils/predictionAdapters.js` exist specifically as named integration points for a future real backend, and currently just return the same mock-derived values as the rest of the app.

**Roles supported (exactly four, defined in `src/auth/roleConfig.js`):**

| Role | Internal id | Represents |
|---|---|---|
| Disaster Authority | `disaster-authority` | The decision-maker with full access |
| Volunteers | `volunteers` | People supporting relocation/shelter logistics |
| Citizen | `citizen` | A resident checking their own safety |
| Emergency Coordinator | `emergency-coordinator` | Runs the operational response |

> **Note on naming:** an earlier version of this project called the Volunteers role "Institution." That role — its label and its internal id — has been fully renamed to Volunteers. The word "Institution" still exists in the app today, but only as the name of an unrelated feature: the **Institution / Evacuation** page (`/app/institution`), which manages evacuation planning for schools, colleges, hospitals, care homes and community centres. That page was never the Volunteers feature and was correctly never renamed.

**Main workflow the UI supports:** hazard zone → affected habitation → habitation risk detail → relocation destination search → safe-site capacity check → allocation → route planning → audit record → national-level rollup.

**Current limitations of mock/static data** are documented in full in [Section I](#i-frontend-limitations).

## USP — Unique Selling Proposition

Most disaster-management tools a district or state actually has access to today are one of two things: a static hazard map with no connection to who lives in the affected area, or a records/reporting system with no map at all. GEOSENTRA's differentiator is not any single feature — it is that the pages below are built to hand off to each other, so a single browsing session can go from "where is the hazard" to "who is affected" to "where can they go" to "how do they get there," without switching tools or re-entering the same location twice. Every point below describes something present in the current frontend prototype today, not a planned feature.

**A. A unified disaster-management interface.** Overview, Hazard Intelligence, Habitations, Safe Sites, Route Intelligence, Institution / Evacuation, and All Relocations Across India are not separate tools — they are pages of one application sharing the same underlying habitation, safe-site, and risk data (`AppStateContext`, `src/data/*.js`), so a number shown on Overview always agrees with what Habitations and Safe Sites show for the same place.

**B. Hazard-to-habitation navigation is a real, working click path, not a mockup.** A map checkpoint (habitation marker) on Hazard Intelligence, a habitation name inside the High Risk box, and a habitation name inside the Moderate Risk box all call the same navigation function and land on that exact habitation's own detail page (`/app/habitations/<slug>`) — confirmed by clicking different items and observing different, correct destinations, not assumed from the code alone.

**C. Relocation-aware Route Intelligence.** Selecting a record on the All Relocations Across India page — or a habitation, a safe site, or an institution's evacuation group elsewhere in the app — opens Route Intelligence pre-loaded with *that specific* source and destination, not a fixed example pair. This is built on the current frontend/mock implementation: the route itself is generated locally between two real coordinates (`src/utils/routing.js`), not returned by a live routing service.

**D. Visual risk prioritization.** Habitation risk is colour-coded consistently everywhere it appears — red for the High Risk box and Critical/High-Risk badges, orange/amber for the Moderate Risk box and Watch-tier badges, green for Normal/Low tier — and safe sites are rendered as a distinct green box marker specifically so they cannot be mistaken for a habitation, hazard, or hospital/school marker at a glance.

**E. Map-based decision support.** The maps let a user see hazard zones, habitations, safe sites, and (on Route Intelligence and the National Relocations map) relocation routes and locations together, and click through to detail on any of them. This supports *planning and review* — it is not live emergency navigation: there is no GPS positioning, no live traffic, and no real routing engine behind it, and the app says so on-screen ("Illustrative route — not a real routing engine").

**F. A role-oriented workflow, not one generic screen.** The application implements exactly four login roles — Disaster Authority, Volunteers, Citizen, and Emergency Coordinator — each seeing a different Overview dashboard and a different, permission-checked set of pages (see [Section B](#b-application-pages) and the access table in the project's role documentation), so a citizen checking their own safety and an authority planning a relocation are not shown the same screen.

**G. A frontend-first, cost-conscious prototype.** The complete user experience described above — every page, every map, every risk calculation — runs using existing frontend components, mock data, and free OpenStreetMap map tiles, with no backend, no database, and no paid API required to build or demonstrate it. This keeps the prototype cheap to build and easy to evaluate, while being honest that it is not yet production-ready (see [Feasibility](#feasibility) below).

> GEOSENTRA's core USP is the integration of hazard awareness, habitation-level risk detail, safe-site identification with real capacity limits, and source-to-destination route intelligence into one role-aware, click-through disaster-management frontend — demonstrated end-to-end today on mock data, and structured so that a real backend and live data sources can be substituted in later without redesigning the interface.

## Feasibility

This section evaluates whether GEOSENTRA can realistically be built, demonstrated, and grown — as a frontend prototype today, and toward a production system later.

### A. Technical feasibility

The current prototype is technically feasible because it is built entirely from mature, freely available frontend tools already present in this repository — nothing described here is aspirational:

| Concern | How it's addressed today |
|---|---|
| UI framework | React 19 (`src/pages`, `src/components`) |
| Build tool | Vite 8 (`npm run dev` / `npm run build`) |
| Routing | react-router-dom v7 — 15 routes plus 1 dynamic habitation route (see [Section C](#c-navigation-and-route-map)) |
| Maps | Leaflet + react-leaflet, on free OpenStreetMap tiles, no API key |
| Styling | Tailwind CSS v4, CSS-first configuration, with a consistent shared component set (`Card`, `Button`, `Badge`, `MetricCard`, `Modal`, …) |
| State/data flow | Three React Contexts (`AuthContext`, `AppStateContext`, `ThemeContext`) — no external state library needed for the app's current size |
| Mock data | Plain JS modules under `src/data/*.js` with small selector functions, easy to later replace with real API calls one function at a time |
| Responsive design | Confirmed working from ~390px mobile width through desktop, with distinct mobile navigation (bottom bar + bottom sheet) and desktop navigation (sidebar) |
| Light/dark mode | Implemented app-wide via `ThemeContext`, persisted locally |
| Source control / hosting | GitHub (this repository) + Vercel, already deployed and working in production |

Because every page, map interaction, risk category, relocation record, and route-display flow in this report is already running in the deployed prototype, technical feasibility for *the frontend prototype* is not a forward-looking claim — it is demonstrated.

### B. Operational feasibility

The current frontend supports the intended review workflow end-to-end: a user can view a role-specific Overview, identify which habitations are Low/Moderate/High Risk or Critical, open a habitation's full detail, locate and compare safe sites against their real capacity limits, review relocation records (per-habitation and, for Disaster Authority, nationwide), and open Route Intelligence to see a source-to-destination route for a specific move.

Usability support already built in includes: colour-coded risk categories used consistently across pages; every meaningful marker and risk-category item being clickable and landing on the correct destination; a structured, role-filtered navigation menu so each role only sees pages relevant to it; and a layout that adapts from desktop tables to mobile card lists rather than breaking down on a small screen.

This demonstrates that the *workflow* is operationally sound for review, training, and demonstration purposes. It has not been tested with real disaster-authority staff or emergency teams, and this report makes no claim that it is in use by any government body or emergency organisation.

### C. Economic feasibility

The prototype stage is cost-conscious by construction: it uses open-source frontend tools (React, Vite, Tailwind, Leaflet), free OpenStreetMap map tiles with no API key or billing account, GitHub for source control, and Vercel for hosting and deployment. No backend server, database, or paid data/API subscription is required to build, run, or demonstrate the current application — mock data stands in for all of these during the prototype stage.

A future production deployment would introduce real costs this report does not attempt to estimate, including: backend application hosting; a managed database; licensing or subscription fees for live hazard/weather data and a real routing/traffic API; authentication infrastructure; monitoring and logging services; and higher-traffic map-tile usage if free-tier limits are exceeded. No specific figures are given here because none currently exist in this project's documentation, and inventing them would misrepresent the prototype's status.

### D. Schedule feasibility

The project is feasible to build incrementally, and the current repository history reflects exactly that phased approach:

1. Frontend interface and navigation — **done**
2. Map and marker implementation — **done**
3. Hazard and habitation interactions (hazard zones, risk tiers, habitation detail) — **done**
4. Safe-site visualization (capacity, bottleneck, suitability) — **done**
5. Relocation records (per-habitation Relocation page, national All Relocations Across India page) — **done**
6. Route Intelligence integration, including relocation-record-aware routing — **done**
7. Responsive/testing pass across roles and viewport sizes — **done for the current feature set**
8. Backend and live-data integration — **not started; a future phase**

Phases 1–7 describe the application as it exists today. Phase 8 is explicitly future work, not partially built.

### E. Scalability feasibility

The current page structure — one detail page per habitation, one card per safe site, one filterable list for national relocation records — is already shaped to hold more data without a redesign. Turning that structural headroom into a scaled, live system would require the following **future enhancements**, none of which exist in the code today:

- Backend integration and a real database, replacing `src/data/*.js`
- Live hazard data feeds (meteorological, geological, satellite)
- IoT/sensor integration for ground-truth conditions
- A trained ML risk-prediction model, replacing the current fixed formula
- Dedicated authority/administrator dashboards beyond the current four roles
- Citizen-submitted reporting
- Real push/SMS/email notifications
- Offline support
- Multilingual support
- Coverage of additional Indian regions beyond the current sample data
- Real-time routing and traffic conditions
- Persistent (not session-only) audit logging
- More granular role-based permissions

### F. Legal, security, and data feasibility

The current prototype uses a mock, local-only session with no password and no server-side check (`AuthContext`, `localStorage`) — this is appropriate for a demonstration and is not appropriate for a production emergency system. Before any real deployment, the project would need: real, secure authentication; enforced role-based access control on a server (not only in the browser, as today); protection of sensitive location and population data; secure API communication (HTTPS, proper auth tokens); input validation on any real data-entry path; documented data-privacy practices; verified and reliable hazard/population data sources; backup and recovery procedures; and persistent monitoring and audit logging. The current frontend prototype should not be presented or deployed as an official emergency-response system until these requirements are addressed.

### G. Overall feasibility conclusion

GEOSENTRA is technically feasible as a frontend prototype, and that feasibility is already demonstrated rather than projected: the core user interface and navigation workflow — hazard awareness, habitation detail, safe-site evaluation, relocation records, and source-to-destination route intelligence — are built and working today, on mock data, deployed via GitHub and Vercel. The same architecture is structured to accept a real backend, live data sources, and more advanced intelligence in future phases without a ground-up rewrite. Moving from this prototype to a system suitable for real production or emergency use would additionally require the validation, reliable data sourcing, security work, and testing described in Sections C, F above — work that has not yet been done and is not claimed to have been done.

### Feasibility summary

| Feasibility area | Current status | Future requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Technical feasibility | Frontend pages, routing, maps, risk categories, and relocation-to-route flow implemented and deployed | Backend and live-data integration |
| Operational feasibility | Users can explore hazards, habitations, safe sites, and relocation records through a role-filtered workflow | Real user testing and authority validation |
| Economic feasibility | Prototype uses open-source frontend tools, free map tiles, GitHub and Vercel — no backend/paid API required | Production infrastructure and service costs (not yet estimated) |
| Schedule feasibility | Frontend built incrementally across 7 completed phases | Additional phase for backend, live data, and further testing |
| Scalability feasibility | Page/data structure can hold more habitations, sites and records without a redesign | Database, real APIs, monitoring, and performance optimisation |
| Security / data feasibility | Prototype-level mock authentication, browser-only session | Production authentication, authorization, privacy, and security controls |

## B. Application pages

Every page below was confirmed by reading `src/App.jsx` and the corresponding component file.

### 1. Landing
- **Route:** `/`
- **Component:** `src/pages/Landing.jsx`
- **Purpose:** Public marketing/pitch page shown before login.

- **User actions:** "Explore Platform" → `/role-select`; "Dashboard" → `/app`; "View Live Demo" → `/app/routes`.
- **Data displayed:** A slice of the real mock habitations/safe sites/hazard zones, purely for visual effect.
- **Related pages:** Role Select.

### 2. Role Select
- **Route:** `/role-select`
- **Component:** `src/pages/RoleSelect.jsx`
- **Purpose:** Choose one of the four roles to start a session.
- **Main UI elements:** Four role cards (icon, label, description) sourced from `ROLE_LABELS` / `ROLE_DESCRIPTIONS`.
- **User actions:** Click a role card → creates a local mock session (`AuthContext.login`) and navigates to `/app`.
- **Data displayed:** None — this page is purely the login gate.
- **Related pages:** Landing, Overview.

### 3. Overview (Dashboard)
- **Route:** `/app` (index route under the authenticated `/app` layout)
- **Component:** `src/pages/Dashboard.jsx`

- **User actions:** Click any tile → navigates to the relevant page; toggle map layers (Hazard Layers / Population / Infrastructure / Safe Sites); click a map marker (see [Section D](#d-map-functionality)); click a Priority Habitation row → Habitation Detail.

- **Route:** `/app/hazard-intelligence`
- **Component:** `src/pages/HazardIntelligence.jsx`

## C. Navigation and route map

All routes are declared in `src/App.jsx` using `react-router-dom` v7 (`<BrowserRouter>`, standard `<Routes>`/`<Route>`). No page uses URL query parameters for its state today — cross-page context is passed through two React Contexts instead (see below), which is this project's existing convention.

| Route | Page/component | Dynamic segment | Query params | Guard (`RoleRoute pageId`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `/` | Landing | — | — | none (public) |
| `/role-select` | RoleSelect | — | — | none (public) |
| `/app` | Dashboard | — | — | none (any authenticated session) |
| `/app/hazard-intelligence` | HazardIntelligence | — | — | `hazard` |
| `/app/habitations` | Habitations | — | — | `habitations` |
| `/app/habitations/:id` | HabitationDetail | `:id` = habitation slug | — | `habitations` |
| `/app/relocation` | Relocation | — | — | `relocation` |
| `/app/safe-sites` | SafeSites | — | — | `sites` |
| `/app/routes` | RouteIntelligence | — | — | `routes` |
| `/app/institution` | Institution | — | — | `evacuation` |
| `/app/what-if` | WhatIf | — | — | `whatif` |
| `/app/alerts` | Alerts | — | — | `alerts` |
| `/app/audit-trail` | AuditTrail | — | — | `audit` |
| `/app/settings` | Settings | — | — | `settings` |
| `/app/national-relocations` | NationalRelocations | — | — | `national-relocations` |
| `*` | Landing (fallback) | — | — | none |

**How cross-page navigation actually carries data** (no query strings involved):

- `AppStateContext` (`src/state/AppStateContext.jsx`) holds `selectedHabitationId`, `selectedSiteId`, `routeOriginOverride` ({kind:'institution', id}), and `customRoute` ({origin, destination} — a one-shot override for an arbitrary named point pair not present in the local habitations/safe-sites arrays).
- Clicking a habitation anywhere calls `selectHabitation(id)` then `navigate('/app/habitations/' + id)`.
- Route Intelligence resolves its origin/destination, on every mount, from — in this priority order — `customRoute` (if set, then immediately cleared) → `routeOriginOverride`/`selectedHabitationId` → the hand-authored default trip.

**Specific behaviours requested for verification:**

- **Hazard Intelligence checkpoint (map marker) clicks** → `openHabitation(id)` → `/app/habitations/<id>`.
- **High Risk box clicks** (any habitation listed inside) → the same `openHabitation(id)` function → `/app/habitations/<id>`.
- **Moderate Risk box clicks** → the same `openHabitation(id)` function → `/app/habitations/<id>`.
- **Habitation Detail navigation** — reached from: Habitations list rows, Overview map markers, Hazard Intelligence map markers, Hazard Intelligence risk boxes, Alerts "Open" action, global header search.
- **Overview navigation** — metric tiles route to Habitations / Safe Sites / Hazard Intelligence depending on the tile; map markers route per marker type (habitation → detail, site → Safe Sites, institution → Institution page).
- **Safe Sites navigation** — "Match Habitation" → Relocation; "Route to This Site" → Route Intelligence with `selectSite(id)` called first.
- **National Relocations navigation** — see [Section E](#e-relocation-workflow).
- **Route Intelligence navigation** — reachable from Safe Sites, Relocation, Institution / Evacuation, and All Relocations Across India, each pre-loading a different origin/destination pair through the mechanism above.
- **Relocation source-to-destination route selection** — on the Relocation page itself, "View Safe Routes" on a ranked match calls `selectSite(siteId)` then navigates to `/app/routes`, which then resolves its destination from that selected site.

---

## D. Map functionality

All maps use the shared `src/components/map/GeoMap.jsx` component, built on `react-leaflet` v5 / `leaflet` v1.9, rendering free OpenStreetMap raster tiles (no API key, no billing). Dark mode is achieved with a CSS filter on the tile layer (`invert/hue-rotate/brightness`), not a second tile server. There are **6 maps** in the codebase: Landing (non-interactive preview), Overview, Hazard Intelligence, Habitation Detail, Route Intelligence, All Relocations Across India. Safe Sites, Relocation, Habitations (list), Institution, What-If, Alerts, Audit Trail and Settings have no map.

No map anywhere uses a true Leaflet popup with buttons inside it — every marker instead shows a small hover tooltip (name only), and a click either navigates directly or opens a page-level modal.

### Overview map (`Dashboard.jsx`)
- **Markers shown:** habitations (red pins — colour is fixed per marker *type*, not per risk tier, even though each marker carries a `priority` field with the habitation's status; `GeoMap.jsx` does not currently read that field for colour), safe sites, and — when the Infrastructure layer is on — shelters/hospitals/schools.
- **Green safe-site boxes:** safe sites render as a distinct rounded-square marker with a white checkmark (`shape: 'box'` on the marker object, drawn by `boxIcon()` in `GeoMap.jsx`), specifically so they are unmistakable from every other marker shape on this map.
- **Hazard marker behaviour:** hazard *zones* (not markers) are drawn as shaded polygons, coloured by severity; toggled by the "Hazard Layers" panel item.
- **Habitation marker behaviour:** click → `openHabitation(id)` → Habitation Detail.
- **Routes:** intentionally absent. The map-layer "Routes" toggle and the route-line rendering were removed from this page; the "Map Layers" panel now only offers Hazard Layers, Population, Infrastructure, and Safe Sites.
- **Click behaviour:** habitation marker → Habitation Detail; safe-site box → `/app/safe-sites`; institution marker (Volunteers' view) → `/app/institution`.
- **Legend:** the four severity dots (Safe / Moderate Risk / High Risk / Red Zone-Critical) plus a fifth entry, a small green square swatch labelled "Safe Sites."

### Hazard Intelligence map (`HazardIntelligence.jsx`)
- **Hazard checkpoints:** shaded hazard-zone polygons; clicking one opens a detail modal (hazard type, affected area, hazard-specific fields, confidence, last-updated, source status) — this does not navigate away from the page.
- **Risk categories:** the on-page High Risk (red) and Moderate Risk (orange) boxes list habitations by tier (High Risk box = Critical + High-Risk status habitations; Moderate Risk box = Watch-status habitations), independent of the map itself.
- **Checkpoint (habitation marker) click behaviour:** → Habitation Detail, identical destination and mechanism as the risk-box clicks.
- **High Risk box behaviour:** click any listed habitation name → its own Habitation Detail page.
- **Moderate Risk box behaviour:** click any listed habitation name → its own Habitation Detail page.
- **Habitation navigation:** confirmed to differ per item — different habitations open different `/app/habitations/<slug>` addresses, not one shared page.

### Route Intelligence map (`RouteIntelligence.jsx`)
- **Source location:** the "From" field — resolved from `customRoute`, `routeOriginOverride`, `selectedHabitationId`, or a hand-authored default.
- **Destination location:** the "To" field — resolved from `customRoute` or `selectedSiteId`, or a hand-authored default.
- **Route display:** up to 3 route lines (Safest/Balanced/Fastest), either the hand-authored default trip (`src/data/routes.js`) or generated on the fly by `generateRoutes()` for any other origin/destination pair.
- **How selected relocation data is passed:** through `AppStateContext`, not a URL query string — see [Section C](#c-navigation-and-route-map).
- **Query/state/parameter behaviour:** state-based (React Context), no query parameters used.
- **Mock or real:** explicitly labelled on screen, "Illustrative route — not a real routing engine." Routes are generated locally by bending a line between two real coordinates and checking which mock hazard-zone polygons it crosses.

### All Relocations Across India map (`NationalRelocations.jsx`)
- **Markers shown:** one per (filtered) relocation record, positioned at that record's real source coordinates, coloured by hazard type.
- **Click behaviour:** opens Route Intelligence pre-loaded with that exact record's source and destination via `setCustomRoute()`.

---

## E. Relocation workflow (All Relocations Across India)

- **Route:** `/app/national-relocations` · **Access:** Disaster Authority only · **Data:** `src/data/nationalRelocations.js`

Each of the 15 mock relocation records carries these actual field names: `id`, `habitation` (source), `source` (`{lat, lng}`), `destination` (name), `destinationPos` (`{lat, lng}`), `district`, `state`, `hazardType`, `relocationType` (Immediate / Short-Term / Medium-Term / Permanent), `peopleCount`, `status` (Planned / In Progress / Completed / Delayed), `startDate`, `authority`, `priority` (Critical / High / Medium / Low).

**Interactions, all wired to the same `openRoute(record)` function:**

| Trigger | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Table row click (desktop) | `openRoute(record)` |
| Explicit "View route" button in the row | `openRoute(record)`, `stopPropagation()`'d so it doesn't double-fire the row click |
| Mobile card click | `openRoute(record)` |
| Map marker click | Looks up the matching record by id from the currently filtered list, then `openRoute(record)` |

**`openRoute(record)` does exactly this:**

```js
setCustomRoute({
  origin: { id: `nr-source-${record.id}`, name: record.habitation, lat: record.source.lat, lng: record.source.lng },
  destination: { id: `nr-dest-${record.id}`, name: record.destination, lat: record.destinationPos.lat, lng: record.destinationPos.lng },
})
navigate('/app/routes')
```

**How the selected source/destination is preserved:** `setCustomRoute` writes into `AppStateContext`, which is a React Context available app-wide — it survives the navigation to Route Intelligence because both pages read from the same provider (mounted once in `src/main.jsx`, above the router). Route Intelligence reads `customRoute` in a `useEffect` on arrival, applies it to its own local origin/destination state, and immediately calls `setCustomRoute(null)` so a later, unrelated navigation to Route Intelligence isn't silently overridden by a stale value.

**How different records produce different routes:** each record supplies its own real `source`/`destinationPos` coordinates, so `generateRoutes()` (`src/utils/routing.js`) computes a genuinely different line, distance and duration per record. Confirmed directly: Meppadi Basti → Kalpetta Relocation Township (Kerala), Puri Coastal Hamlets → Bhubaneswar Rehabilitation Colony (Odisha), Uttarkashi Ridge Hamlets → Dehradun Transit Camp (Uttarakhand), and Majuli Char Settlements → Jorhat Mainland Township (Assam) each produced a distinct, correct route.

---

## F. Risk and habitation workflow

**Risk tiers** (`REDZONE_STATUS` in `src/types/geosentra.js`), from the shared formula in `src/utils/riskCalculations.js`:

| Status | Default score range | Colour | Relocation timeframe |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normal (shown as "Low Risk" on Overview) | 0–39 | Green | Monitor Only |
| Watch (shown as "Moderate Risk") | 40–64 | Amber | Medium-Term |
| High Risk | 65–84 | Orange/Red | Short-Term |
| Critical Red Zone | 85–100 | Dark red | Immediate |

Risk score formula: `Hazard Intensity × 0.40 + Population Vulnerability × 0.25 + Disaster History × 0.20 + Infrastructure Constraint × 0.15`, then pulled slightly toward the midpoint when the habitation's own data confidence is low.

**High Risk behaviour:** the Hazard Intelligence "High Risk" box lists every habitation whose status is Critical Red Zone or High Risk; clicking one opens `/app/habitations/<slug>`.
**Moderate Risk behaviour:** the "Moderate Risk" box lists every habitation whose status is Watch; same click behaviour.
**Map checkpoint behaviour:** identical destination and function (`openHabitation`) as the risk boxes — deliberately kept consistent.
**Habitation Detail behaviour and actions:** see page 6 in [Section B](#b-application-pages).

**Role restrictions confirmed by testing, not just by reading the permission table:**
- Citizens and Volunteers do not have the `habitations` permission. A Citizen's own Overview map still shows a marker for their home area, and a Volunteer can still see habitation names inside the Hazard Intelligence risk boxes — clicking either correctly renders the Access Restricted screen rather than crashing, since neither role can open `/app/habitations/:id`.

## G. UI and design system

Confirmed directly in `src/index.css`, `vite.config.js`, and the shared `src/components/ui/*` files. There is **no `tailwind.config.js`** — this project uses Tailwind CSS v4's CSS-first configuration (`@import "tailwindcss"` + a single `@theme` block).

**Typography:** `Inter` (declared as `--font-sans` in the `@theme` block), falling back to system UI sans-serif fonts. One typeface is used throughout the whole application — no serif or monospace display face.

**Palette (as actually used across components, not a design-token file — Tailwind utility classes are used directly):**

| Purpose | Light | Dark |
|---|---|---|
| Page background | `#f4f7fc` | `#0b1220` |
| Primary accent / primary buttons | Tailwind `blue-600` | Tailwind `blue-600` (same, on darker surfaces) |
| "Good" / safe status | Tailwind `emerald-*` | `emerald-400`-family |
| "Warning" / moderate status | Tailwind `amber-*` | `amber-400`-family |
| "Danger" / high-critical status | Tailwind `red-*` | `red-400`-family |
| Surfaces / cards | white, `slate-200/70` border | `slate-900`, `slate-800` border |
| Map tiles (dark mode) | — | same OSM tiles, CSS `invert/hue-rotate/brightness/contrast/saturate` filter applied to the tile pane only |

**Status colours used on maps and badges:**
- Green box marker with white checkmark = safe site (new this cycle).
- Red pin = habitation marker (fixed colour, does not vary by risk tier today — see Section D).
- Hazard-zone severity fill: green (Safe) → amber (Moderate Risk) → orange (High Risk) → dark red (Red Zone/Critical).
- Hazard Intelligence risk boxes: solid **red** border/icon for the High Risk box, solid **amber/orange** border/icon for the Moderate Risk box (`src/pages/HazardIntelligence.jsx`, `RISK_BOX_STYLE`).

**Light/dark mode:** implemented via a `dark` class on `<html>`, toggled by `ThemeContext` (`src/context/ThemeContext.jsx`), persisted to `localStorage`, defaulting to the OS `prefers-color-scheme`. Every shared UI component (`Card`, `Button`, `Badge`, `MetricCard`, `Modal`, …) declares both a light and a `dark:` variant with Tailwind's `dark:` prefix.

**Layout:** a fixed left `Sidebar` (desktop, `lg:` breakpoint and up) plus a sticky `TopBar` with global search, alerts, theme toggle and profile menu; below `lg:`, the sidebar is replaced by a bottom `MobileNav` (5 primary items + a "More" bottom sheet) and, on Route Intelligence specifically, a draggable `BottomSheet` in place of the fixed side panel.

**Responsive behaviour:** every data-heavy page (Habitations, All Relocations Across India) renders a `<table>` on `md:` and above and a stacked card list below `md:`; stat-tile grids collapse from 4/5 columns to 2 columns on narrow screens; the Overview/Hazard Intelligence/Route Intelligence/National Relocations maps all keep working zoom, pan and marker interaction at any width, confirmed at a 390px viewport.

## H. Technical implementation

Only technology actually present in `package.json` / the source tree is listed here.

| Category | Technology | Version (from `package.json`) |
|---|---|---|
| UI framework | React | ^19.2.8 |
| Build tool / dev server | Vite | ^8.2.2 (`@vitejs/plugin-react`) |
| Routing | react-router-dom | ^7.18.3 (`BrowserRouter`) |
| Map rendering | Leaflet + react-leaflet | ^1.9.4 / ^5.0.0 |
| Map tiles | OpenStreetMap raster tiles | free, no key |
| Styling | Tailwind CSS | ^4.3.3, CSS-first config, no `tailwind.config.js` |
| Icons | lucide-react | ^1.43.0 |
| State management | React Context only — `AuthContext`, `AppStateContext`, `ThemeContext` (no Redux/Zustand/other library) | — |
| Data fetching | None — no `fetch`/`axios`/data-fetching library anywhere in the source | — |
| Mock data structure | Plain JS modules under `src/data/*.js`, each exporting arrays/objects and small selector functions (`getHabitation(id)`, `getSafeSite(id)`, etc.) | — |
| Deployment config | `vercel.json` (single SPA rewrite: `/(.*) → /index.html`) + `.vercel/project.json` (project link) | — |

**Source tree (`src/`):** `assets/`, `auth/` (AuthContext, ProtectedRoute, roleConfig), `components/` (`layout/`, `map/`, `ui/`), `context/` (ThemeContext), `data/` (all mock datasets), `layouts/` (DashboardLayout), `pages/` (every route's component), `state/` (AppStateContext), `types/` (geosentra.js — shared enums/JSDoc shapes), `utils/` (risk/capacity/relocation/route calculations, alerts, search, geo, predictionAdapters).

## I. Frontend limitations

All confirmed by reading the code — none are assumed.

- **No backend / server** — every calculation runs in the browser.
- **No live database** — all data lives in `src/data/*.js` and resets to those values on every page load.
- **No live ML inference** — `src/utils/predictionAdapters.js` contains only mock pass-through functions, each commented `// FUTURE BACKEND INTEGRATION`.
- **No live disaster API** — hazard zones, habitations, safe sites, institutions, and national relocation records are all hand-authored mock arrays.
- **Mock/static route data** — routes are generated locally (`src/utils/routing.js`) or hand-authored (`src/data/routes.js`); there is no real street-network routing engine or live traffic/road-closure feed.
- **No real accounts** — logging in creates a local, unauthenticated session in `localStorage` (`SESSION_STORAGE_KEY = 'geosentra_mock_session'`); there is no password and no server-side check.
- **No persistent audit trail** — session-generated Audit Trail entries are lost on refresh.
- **Risk Score thresholds in Settings are display-only** — not wired into the actual scoring formula.
- **No real push notifications** — Alerts are recomputed on render, not pushed via SMS/email/browser notification.
- **Habitation markers don't change colour by risk tier** — the underlying data is attached to each marker but `GeoMap.jsx` does not currently read it.

## Documentation maintenance checklist

Anyone changing the frontend must update this file **in the same change**, per these rules:

- [ ] **Any new page** → add it to [Section B](#b-application-pages) and to the [Section C](#c-navigation-and-route-map) route table.
- [ ] **Any route path change** → update the route table in Section C and the page it belongs to in Section B.
- [ ] **Any map marker/category change** (new marker type, new colour meaning, new legend item) → update [Section D](#d-map-functionality).
- [ ] **Any navigation change** (a click now goes somewhere different, or a new click target is added) → update the affected page's "User actions" in Section B and the relevant bullet in Section C.
- [ ] **Any change to mock data that affects what's visibly shown** (new/removed habitation, safe site, hazard zone, institution, or national relocation record; new/removed field) → update the relevant page section and, if field names are quoted, [Section E](#e-relocation-workflow) or the data-structure notes in [Section H](#h-technical-implementation).
- [ ] **Any change to deployment configuration** (`vercel.json`, hosting, domain) → update [Section J](#j-deployment-information).
- [ ] **Any removed feature** → delete it from this file; do not leave it described as current. If in doubt, search this file for the feature's name before committing.
- [ ] **USP section updated** when project differentiators change (a page is added/removed, a cross-page navigation flow changes, or a risk/safety visual convention changes).
- [ ] **Feasibility section updated** when the technical scope, tech stack, or deployment setup changes.
- [ ] This file must describe **only the current implementation** — no planned/future features described as done. Planned work belongs in [Section I](#i-frontend-limitations) or a future roadmap note, clearly labelled as not yet built.
- [ ] Before committing, run `npm run docs:check` (see `scripts/check-documentation.mjs`) to catch obvious drift — missing routes, a stale removed-feature phrase, or a missing deployment URL. It is a lightweight sanity check, not a substitute for actually reading the diff against this file.

A companion presentation document, `docs/geosentra-field-guide.html` (also published as a Claude Artifact), covers the same material in a longer, narrative, non-technical form for demos and judging. When a change here is significant enough to matter to that audience (a new page, a changed role, a changed workflow), update that file too and republish it — this Markdown file remains the authoritative, git-tracked source either way.
